newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Alliance & Leicester names float day.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Alliance & Leicester names float day.

text.p: Britain's saving and loans Alliance & Leicester Building Society on Monday announced record profits and said it had set April 21 provisionally as the date for its planned flotation.

Sweeping changes in the sector this year sees four major building societies seeking to shed their mutual status and go public to continue moves into general banking from their traditional domains of mortgage lending and saving.
Customers are set to benefit from hefty share handouts on conversion and some economists fear the influx of cash into the economy could force interest rates higher.
Alliance & Leicester's borrowing and saving members will get 250 shares each although the company said it had not yet decided on the cut-off date for members to be eligible for free shares.

The Alliance & Leicester announcement came as shareholders from Britain's largest building society, the Halifax, gathered to vote on whether its 12 billion sterling ($19.5 billion) conversion should go ahead.
The only other society to float has been the Abbey National Plc, which has become a successful bank since going public in 1989.

The Alliance & Leicester, one of the country's top three building societies with over 24 billion sterling of assets, said over 35 percent of record underlying profit of 359 million sterling in 1996 was generated by non-traditional business.
"This reflects how far the Alliance & Leicester has moved from its original building society roots and the relevance of its decision to convert," the company said.

Group chief executive Peter White said the company would aim to develop pensions and general insurance further in 1997 to build on what he called Alliance & Leicester's well-diversified business. Life assurance and unit trusts products made a profit in their first year, the company said.
White said his group's fourth consecutive year of record profits meant it was well positioned to face life as a public limited company.

In 1996, group pretax profit rose six percent to 306 million sterling. Underlying profit before conversion costs and other items was up 10 percent at 359 million with mortgage lending and investments businesses accounting for 229 million.
Gross mortgage advances dropped to 2.2 billion sterling from 2.9 billion a year earlier but loans in the second half were up 41 percent as the housing market began to recover.

Alliance & Leicester said it had opted to maintain profitability amid aggressive pricing by rivals. As a result, its share of British gross lending dropped to 3.1 percent from 5.2 percent a year earlier although that picked up to 3.5 percent in the last quarter.
The society said it had incurred exceptional administrative costs of 26 million sterling for conversion, including the costs of sending transfer documents to more than three million members.

The Alliance & Leicester plan is set to further fuel debate about whether flotation will actually benefit customers. News headlines have trumpeted likely handouts -- with each qualifying member at the Halifax estimated to get a share windfall worth around 1,000 pounds -- but there have been opponents.

The Halifax Action Group claims borrowers and savers will be worse off if the Halifax goes public. Also, the Halifax's plans have drawn fire from supporters of the disabled because it pays out only to the first-named person on any account. Many disabled people have accounts held on trust by guardians or carers. The Alliance & Leicester's members have already approved conversion. ($ = 0.614 British Pounds Sterling)
